title: Complexe de De Rham à puissance divisée [conférence de 1976 à l’IHÉS] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, taken from the previous page: we work in the category of PD-algebras (A, J, γ). The previous page lists the axioms in full: γ^0 = 1, γ^1 = id, γ^p(x+y) = Σ γ^i(x)γ^j(y), γ^p(λx) = λ^p γ^p(x), γ^pγ^q = binom(p+q,p) γ^{p+q}, and γ^p∘γ^q = (pq)!/((p!)^q q!) γ^{pq}.

Grothendieck now takes a functor F on modules (later presumably on complexes). F is assumed 'compatible with ⊗', meaning it carries natural maps F(P)⊗F(Q) → F(P⊗Q). In modern terms F is lax (symmetric) monoidal, so it sends algebras to algebras: given P⊗Q → R one gets F(P)⊗F(Q) → F(P⊗Q) → F(R).

The universal property of the divided power algebra Γ^*(F(X)) then gives a homomorphism of graded algebras u_*^X : Γ^*F(X) → F(Γ^*(X)), with components u_p^X : Γ^pF(X) → F(Γ^p X). This map is the identity F(X) → F(X) in degree 1.

For x ∈ F(X) he defines x^{(p)} := u_p^X(γ^p x). He then checks that the operations x ↦ x^{(p)} inherit the PD axioms purely from u_* being an algebra map:
- Sum: (x+y)^{(p)} = u_*(γ^p(x+y)) = Σ u(γ^i x)u(γ^j y) = Σ x^{(i)}y^{(j)}.
- Scalars: (λx)^{(p)} = u_p(λ^pγ^p x) = λ^p x^{(p)}.
- Products: x^{(p)}x^{(q)} = u(γ^pγ^q x) = c_{p,q} x^{(p+q)}, with c_{p,q} = binom(p+q,p).

Below the blue line he asks two questions:
- Is u_* 'multilinéaire graduée', and is it compatible with d and the PD structures? This is relevant if F involves complexes, as in the PD de Rham complex.
- Is F Γ^*(X) itself a PD-algebra?

He starts on the last axiom, the composition γ^q∘γ^p. He draws the square Γ^pF(X) → FΓ^p(X), with vertical maps γ^q_{Γ^pF(X)} and F(γ^q_{Γ^p(X)}), going down to Γ^qΓ^pF(X), then to Γ^{qp}F(X) via the canonical comparison map, and to F(Γ^qΓ^p X). The square is left unfinished.

Purpose: show that an F transporting algebras to algebras also transports PD-structures. This is a step toward PD structures on de Rham / Čech-type complexes built functorially, e.g. from Γ_A(X) or from a PD-envelope.
errors: The vertical map F(γ^q_{Γ^p(X)}) applies F to the non-additive (degree-q polynomial) map γ^q. For a functor defined only on linear maps this makes no sense unless F extends to polynomial laws or the map is mediated by Γ^q. This is exactly the gap the unfinished square would have to address.

Showing that the elements x^{(p)} satisfy the first three PD axioms does not make F(Γ^*X) a PD-algebra. The divided powers would have to be defined on all of F(Γ^{≥1}X), not only on images of γ^p(x), so the question 'F Γ^*(X) est-il un p.d.?' remains open on the page.
Compatibility with the composition axiom γ^q∘γ^p is not verified; the diagram is left incomplete.

ideas.what: A tensor-compatible (lax monoidal) functor sends algebras to algebras and induces a natural algebra map Γ^*F(X) → F(Γ^*X), with divided-power operations x^{(p)} = u_p(γ^p x) inheriting the PD axioms.
ideas.modern_name: Divided powers transported along lax symmetric monoidal functors. A classical instance is the shuffle (Eilenberg–Zilber) map giving strictly commutative DG algebras with divided powers, as for the normalization of simplicial commutative rings.
ideas.usually_credited_to: H. Cartan (Séminaire Cartan 1954–55), Eilenberg–MacLane; later Illusie (Complexe cotangent), Berthelot–Ogus for PD de Rham

ideas.what: Verification of the PD axioms for x^{(p)} via the universal property of Γ.
ideas.modern_name: Universal property of the divided power algebra Γ_A(M) (Roby)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine scratch verifications that lax monoidal functors carry divided-power structure. The results are classical (Cartan, Roby, Illusie), and the open question at the end is standard and well understood in the simplicial/DG setting.
transcription_corrections: The line '(x·y)^{(p)} = Σ_{i+j=p} x^{(i)}y^{(j)}' should read '(x+y)^{(p)}'. The image shows a sum, consistent with the formula. Likewise 'u_*(γ_p(x·y))' should be 'u_*(γ^p(x+y))'.
The coefficient written 'c_{p,q}' (rendered like 'q_{p,q}' in the hand) is the binomial coefficient binom(p+q,p) from the previous page.
The blue line 'F(X) –id→ F(X)' denotes the degree-1 component of u_*. 'multi. linéaire graduée' is uncertain; it may read 'multi. linéaire, graduée'.
The bottom right note reads 'F Γ^*(X) est-il un p.d. ?' (with an arrow pointing to the diagram).
